title: UBC launches the first free open-access Nepali textbook - Faculty of Arts
content:
"Introduction to the Nepali Language is the first free open-access textbook of its kind designed for learners, educators, community groups, and heritage speakers of Nepali.  The book was launched in celebration of BC’s first-ever Nepali Heritage Day on 30 May, 2026, marking an important milestone in expanding opportunities for Nepali language learning and engagement.

Developed within the Faculty of Arts, the textbook was created through a collaboration between faculty, students, and staff. The team included principal investigator Dr. Mark Turin, an Associate Professor in the Department of Anthropology and the Institute for Critical Indigenous Studies; Binod Shrestha, an instructor with the Himalaya Program; and Salina Dolmo Lama, a Nepali graduate student at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs.

The project also received support from the Open Education Resources (OER) Affordability Grant Program and was enhanced by contributions from the UBC Library’s Scholarly Communications team and open education infrastructure supported by the Centre for Teaching, Learning and Technology (CTLT)."

title: Investing $4.9 million of our surplus in rebuilding the Crossref system - Crossref
content:
"The infrastructure that registers and distributes Crossref metadata has been running and growing for more than two decades. It now does considerably more than it was built to do, and it shows: two large, tightly coupled monoliths (Content System and REST API), where a change in one place risks breaking something in another.

In its July meeting, the Crossref board approved the use of Crossref surplus funds for a three-year project to accelerate the redesign of the Crossref system. Our plan is to use $1.6 million a year for three years (~USD $4.9M in total) from our surplus funds, which will help us set up a modern infrastructure consisting of separate services for the different functionalities that the Crossref system offers."

title: Not All Research Environments are Created Equal: Structural Injustice in Low-Resourced Scientific Settings and Its Epistemic Implications
content: Abstract: This paper discusses three forms of structural injustice associated with disparities in the resources available to researchers, and the opportunity researchers have to pursue their scientific goals. These are: (1) resource injustice; (2) focus injustice; and (3) labour injustice. I argue that such structural injustice has significant epistemic implications, resulting in: shifts in research content; the exclusion of substantive portions of scientific community from contributing to knowledge production to the best of their abilities; the exclusion of specific methods and data sources from global scientific discourse, on grounds other than scientific quality and relevance; a loss of quality and reliability in processes and outcomes of inquiry; and the inability to implement openness and related forms of constructive scrutiny. To exemplify these forms of injustice and their epistemic implications, I discuss everyday challenges within life science sites in Italy, Ghana and Greece, as documented through ethnographic research. content: "But given the many different ways to connect in the Fediverse—why do almost all academic associations or institutions choose a Mastodon server, of all things, for their communities? Bonfire isn’t a platform or an “app,” but rather a modular framework for building digital community spaces. Possible features include feeds (that interact with or federate with Mastodon, etc.), groups, user circles, and moderation tools… and if something is missing, you can develop it (or have it developed). title: Open practices across science, software, education and other domains | Nature Human Behaviour
content: Abstract:  Open practices are actions people perform to influence transparency (who can see information), inclusion (who can voice perspectives) and decision rights (who can make decisions). Open practices have grown popular across domains, including open science, open-source software and open education, in hopes of spurring innovation and broadening participation. But which open practices best enable groups and organizations to achieve these ambitious goals, and why? This Perspective distils seven successful practices from across these domains that can help groups to define goals, allocate power, share information and set norms. These practices, such as documenting power structures and adopting a code of conduct, hold potential to support groups and organizations seeking to address great challenges through openness. However, delivering on that potential will depend on how well groups share lessons across domains, tailor these practices and sustain the people and platforms that carry them.

title: On the Open Science Framework's changes - Chris Hartgerink, PhD
content:
"The OSF was pivotal to the early days of reforming research around 2012-2017. I used it a lot for a while, and ultimately used it through its integrations only. It added some great services and some not so great ones. I did not always agree with their approach, but I was often glad they existed.

The OSF has had many failings over the years and I think it is great they're making a decision on the role it has in 2026 and beyond. To me, the decision to unwind projects is a reflection of the fact that they did not really connect with the userbase to understand the needs of researchers, while riding on the tide that they served the researcher's needs. They gobbled up tens of millions of dollars for their operations. The fact that this announcement came as a surprise, is a highlight of how disconnected the development was from the people they claim to serve."

content: "The Center for Open Science (COS) has announced a significant change for the Open Science Framework (OSF). title: OSF is Changing: What's changing, what's continuing, and where to find guidance
content: "We are preparing substantial changes to OSF that will reduce its functionality, focus OSF on its unique strengths, and move toward an integrated model with complementary services like Zenodo, a repository for researchers to share data, materials, and code hosted by CERN, for researchers to do open science. As part of that shift, the OSF Projects workflow – the part of the OSF used for project collaboration, file management, and storage – is being phased out as an active workspace. This change does not affect persistence and accessibility of existing public projects. We are very sorry for the disruption that this will cause for OSF users. These changes are necessary because of a challenging funding environment for open research infrastructure. Important background about why we are making this change is available in a separate post. Our priorities are to support the long-term discovery and access of content publicly shared on OSF so it remains persistent, discoverable, and accessible, and to ease the transition for users to continue doing open science. title: Librarians as Creators of Open Educational Resources for Advanced Searching
content: Abstract:  Health librarians are increasingly authoring their own open educational resources (OERs) to teach advanced literature searching—an essential skill for evidence synthesis. These instructional materials, often created in response to gaps in existing resources, go beyond simple guides incorporating bilingual content, scaffolded exercises, knowledge checks, and video tutorials. They reflect librarians’ deep expertise and commitment to affordable, open, and high-quality learning materials. This panel will explore three librarian-led OER projects that exemplify this growing trend. Through brief presentations and a moderated discussion, panelists will share insights into the design, implementation, and impact of their work, and reflect on the broader implications of OER creation as a scholarly and pedagogical practice.

title: University libraries between cost-cutting measures and open access transformation
content: From Google's English:  “When considering the financial resources of university libraries, two fundamental developments must be distinguished, both of which impact their budgets,” explains André Karliczek, Deputy Director of the Thuringian University and State Library Jena (ThULB). “Firstly, these libraries, whose core mission is providing information for study, research, and teaching, are increasingly becoming the primary bearers of publication costs in the course of the open access transformation – particularly within the framework of the DEAL agreements – because publishers have shifted their business model from subscription to open access publication. Acquisition budgets are therefore no longer solely used to purchase and license literature, but increasingly also to finance publication fees. Secondly, the changed economic conditions imposed by the federal and state governments necessitate the management of reduced expenditures – though to very different degrees depending on the specific area of ​​responsibility and the federal state.”

title: Beyond metric reductionism: assessment creep as an emerging risk of research evaluation reform | Research Evaluation | Oxford Academic
content: Abstract:  Recent research assessment reforms have successfully challenged the overreliance on simplistic quantitative indicators and promoted broader approaches to evaluation. This paper argues that these reforms may also generate a new risk: assessment creep, understood as the gradual accumulation of evaluation criteria without sufficient attention to how they are prioritised and combined. While criteria such as open science, societal impact, international collaboration, leadership, and mentoring may each be valuable, their proliferation can reduce transparency and make evaluation systems more difficult to understand and scrutinise. Less transparent systems may also make it harder to distinguish legitimate expert judgement from arbitrary decision-making and to detect favouritism or other forms of unwarranted advantage. Drawing on recent debates surrounding responsible research assessment, the paper suggests that the next challenge is not choosing between metrics and expert judgement, but designing evaluation systems that remain coherent, transparent, and accountable as they become increasingly complex.

title: TOP 2025: An update to the Transparency and Openness Promotion Guidelines - PhilPapers
content: Abstract: BackgroundTransparency and openness are core scientific values that enable independent verification of reported research results. The Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, first published in 2015 (TOP 2015), provided a flexible framework for journals to design and implement publication standards promoting these values. Over the past decade, widespread use of TOP 2015 contributed to valuable evidence and feedback for refinement.Main TextThe TOP Advisory Board undertook a comprehensive update of TOP 2015 that went into effect in 2025 (TOP 2025). The update introduces an explicit conceptual framework clarifying its primary objective: improving the verifiability of empirical research claims. Standards are reorganized into three categories (Research Practices, Verification Practices, and Verification Studies) that resolve conceptual and structural limitations of TOP 2015. title: How a Diamond Open Access Publisher Expanded into Open Textbooks - Pressbooks
content:
The University of Groningen Press (UGP) is a Diamond Open Access university press based in the Netherlands and a member of the Netherlands University Presses (NUPs) network. Since its founding in 2017, the press has supported the publication of Diamond Open Access scholarly journals and books.

In 2021, UGP expanded into a closely related—but distinct—area of open publishing by launching an open textbook pilot. As part of the University’s broader commitment to open education and open science, the initiative explored how UGP could apply its scholarly publishing expertise and open infrastructure to help faculty create high-quality open textbooks and other open educational resources.

What began as a pilot has since developed into an institutional service supporting multiple models of textbook production, enabling collaboration across institutions, and supporting the creation of interactive learning materials designed for teaching and learning contexts.

title: Panel: Hoe maken we Open Science echt gelijkwaardig?
content: How can science and knowledge production become more open, inclusive and equitable? This is not only a question of access to existing knowledge, but also of agency: who formulates research questions, who is recognised as a knowledge producer, and which forms of knowledge are considered legitimate? During the Netherlands National Open Science Week, Leiden University’s three UNESCO Chairs will come together to discuss these questions. The Chairs maintain broad international networks and collaborate with researchers and knowledge communities in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Their work covers diversity in science, digital diversity, colonial history, and collaboration with societal and international knowledge communities. The central question of the panel is how researchers, universities and research funders can contribute to more equitable international collaboration. The panellists will also critically examine the distribution of resources, authorship, theoretical authority and institutional recognition. title: Risks and possibilities in sharing preprints during the doctorate - University of Southern Denmark
content: Abstract:  During doctoral candidature, students may seek to publish journal articles, which they may incorporate in their thesis if their institutional policy permits. They may consider sharing pre-prints of these texts either pre- or post-publication to promote open access and knowledge mobilisation. There is very little extant research that explores doctoral students’ knowledge of the risks and possibilities involved in sharing their work in this form, and this chapter seeks to identify those that they could encounter. It offers immediate value for informing doctoral education and a useful foundation for future research that is specific to the doctoral student experience.

content: Abstract: The shift from closed scholarship to open science has sparked the importance of Research Data Management (RDM) in supporting Open Access (OA) in academic institutions. This paper explores the perceptions of academic librarians on RDM practices for promoting OA in South African universities. title: The Crisis of Scholarly Communication in the Open Access Environment: Pathways to Diamond Open Access[v1] | Preprints.org
content: Abstract: This paper presents a critical analysis of the current system of scholarly communication, which has undergone a profound transformation under the influence of excessive commercialization within the neoliberal "publish or perish" paradigm. The study demonstrates that the Open Access movement, in its current form, has been co-opted by major commercial publishers through mechanisms such as Article Processing Charges (APCs) and "Transformative Agreements," which fail to solve the problem of creating a fair and accessible environment for the dissemination of knowledge. The work substantiates the thesis that the prestige of academic journals has ceased to be a reliable indicator of scientific quality, and that the traditional peer-review system is in a state of crisis, driven by the exponential growth of publications and a catastrophic shortage of qualified reviewers. The author analyzes potential solutions to this impasse, including a transition to platform-based publication and review models, as well as the advancement of Diamond Open Access. title: Who Owns Discovery? Academic Capitalism, Prestige Markets, and the Enclosure of Science
content: Abstract: Academic publishing rests on an institutional paradox that borders on the absurd. Public institutions finance much of the research and universities pay the scientists; those scientists then write the papers and typically supply peer review without compensation from publishers, while publishers often acquire exclusive rights and sell access back to the institutions that provided both the knowledge and the evaluative labor. Smaller universities and peripheral research systems contribute to a global scholarly record that their libraries may struggle to afford, while their researchers face a second barrier when publication itself carries a fee. This article reconstructs how that arrangement emerged through the history of publishing, the sociology of science, industrial organization, research evaluation, open access, and the political economy of artificial intelligence. title: Examining Persistence of European Open Repository Infrastructure and its Diffusion in the Scholarly Record – InfoDoc MicroVeille

title: arXiv welcomes inaugural CEO and founding Board of Directors
content: "We have exciting news to share today: the appointment of Dr. Penelope Lewis as arXiv’s inaugural Chief Executive Officer and the establishment of our Board of Directors. If you’ve been following arXiv’s transition to an independent nonprofit organization, these leadership appointments mark a significant step in our journey. Having a CEO and Board in place strengthens our governance, sustainability, and capacity to serve the global research community for generations to come. For more than three decades, arXiv has enabled rapid and open sharing of scientific research. It has operated largely on the support and dedication of its staff, moderators, volunteers, members, funders, and, for the past 25 years, the institutional backing of Cornell. As the scale, reach, and importance of the platform have grown, so too has the need for more formal leadership and governance structures that support long-term sustainability. The appointment of the first CEO and creation of an international governing board reflect our commitment to maintaining arXiv as a trusted, community-centered resource while preparing for future opportunities and evolution. title: NIH Director Bhattacharya kills more health disparities grants | Science | AAAS
content:
"Now, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya is ending two more grants, both for health disparities research at the University of Pittsburgh (Pitt).

A 4 August letter sent by Bhattacharya to Pitt’s research office informing it that a grant to social epidemiologist Tamara Dubowitz “will be terminated in full” confirms that more cancellations are coming...Her 5-year, NIH-funded study exploring health and socioeconomic factors contributing to cognitive aging and Alzheimer’s in African Americans living in poor neighborhoods in Pittsburgh is nearing completion, and her team has already spent $7 million of the $9.6 million grant. She says neither her project nor the other Pitt grant slated to be killed were given a chance to adjust their research to comply with new NIH priorities Bhattacharya has detailed."

title: Choosing What’s Next: Introducing the National Open Education Priorities Process — Open Education Association
content: "Open education is more relevant to the problems facing higher education than ever before, yet it is too often absent from the rooms where decisions are made. Twenty years of OER advocacy successfully made the case against expensive textbooks. That case still holds, but it no longer opens every door it used to. This fall, the Open Education Association invites the open education field to collaborate on a process to choose national priorities: specific problems that higher education leaders and policymakers are already trying to solve, where open education offers a solution. Examples could include how to train nurses faster by reducing cost as a barrier, how to break down silos in educational data, or how to improve AI literacy through open materials. Working collaboratively across the field, this process will surface a list of potential priorities, discuss them throughout the fall, and select the final priorities at a national summit in November. This webinar will officially kick off the process and explain how it will work, including what we mean by national priorities, how to join or host a listening session, and how to apply to serve as a representative at a national summit this

title: NOT-OD-26-100: Implementation Update: NIH Data Management and Sharing Plan Requirements
content: "This Guide Notice provides an update to the research community on forms changes when NIH transitions to the updated Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Plan format which includes reporting changes to previously approved DMS Plans. Background The NIH Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Policy ensures that the benefits of taxpayer funded research are maximally shared to advance research, improve health outcomes, and cultivate trust in the biomedical research enterprise. When released in 2023, NIH issued supplemental information outlining desired elements of a DMS Plan. After several years of implementation experience, NIH issued Notice NOT-OD-26-046, Updated Elements of an NIH Data Management and Sharing Plan, to provide a structured template and format across all NIH Institutes, Centers, and Offices (ICOs.) NIH is finalizing implementation of this new format to ensure NIH's data sharing goals are achieved while reducing administrative burden and improving reporting efficiency. The planned updates to the DMS Plan format do not constitute a change in NIH policy. title: USRN September Community Call - Shared Repository Services
content:
"Repositories are key institutional tools that ensure access to and reuse of valuable research outputs. To better support those goals, some institutions have developed or use shared repository services. USRN is bringing together a panel to discuss their use cases and experiences of shared repository services.

Panelists will share how the conversations about shared repository services started and evolved at their institution, who was involved, and what services are now being utilized. This conversation aims to share the experiences of those using shared repositories services (without digging into the technical implementation) and to gauge interest in the topic for future conversations."

title: ADOPTION OF OPEN ACCESS PUBLISHING AMONG LIBRARIANS IN FEDERAL UNIVERSITIES IN NORTH-CENTRAL NIGERIA: MODERATING ROLES OF PUBLISHING BEHAVIOUR AND RESEARCH ASSESSMENT PRACTICES
content: "This study examined the adoption of Open Access (OA) publishing among librarians and Library and Information Science (LIS) educators in federal universities in North-Central Nigeria, with particular attention to the moderating roles of publishing behaviour and research assessment practices. A systematic review design was adopted to synthesise empirical and theoretical literature published between 2020 and 2026. Relevant sources were retrieved from Google Scholar, Web of Science, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), and the extracted data were analysed using thematic content analysis guided by the PRISMA protocol. Findings showed that the level of OA adoption among librarians and LIS educators is moderate but increasing, driven by awareness of visibility, accessibility, and global dissemination benefits associated with open scholarship. The review further established that publishing behaviour significantly shapes OA adoption, with librarians who hold favourable attitudes toward research productivity, scholarly collaboration, and digital publishing being more inclined to engage with OA outlets. title: Open Science in a Changing World—The Open Science Festival 2027 Takes Shape - pulse49.com
content:
"Open Science is often discussed in terms of principles: transparency, accessibility, participation and collaboration. The decisive question, however, is how these principles can be translated into research practice—particularly at a time when the conditions under which knowledge is produced, communicated and trusted are changing rapidly.

On 18 and 19 March 2027, the fifth Open Science Festival in the German-speaking world will bring this discussion to the University of Bamberg. The festival will provide a platform for researchers, early-career scholars, students, citizen scientists, and staff from libraries, infrastructure organisations and research institutions to exchange experiences and develop new perspectives on open scholarship."

title: Programme plan SPII Part 2 | Zenodo
content: SPII-2 is set up as a co-production programme, involving key stakeholders from research institutions, infrastructure providers and national initiatives. The programme is structured along five interrelated lines of approach: · [A] Development of additional use cases to potentially expand the requirements for OSI · [B] Technical setup - developing a reference model and interoperability requirements · [C] Connecting and collaborating with infrastructures (existing and in development) · [D] Organisational and financial models for the federation · [E] Explorative study – assessing the impact of emerging technologies (e.g. AI, decentralised models) These lines are strongly interdependent and will be coordinated and integrated by a core group. This programme plan is in development and will be updated periodically to reflect discussions with the various stakeholders: · In version 0.4 the descriptions of lines B and C have been revised · In an additional chapter (Chapter 6. title: OMB grant regulation paused by Congress - STM Association
content: "The US Senate has taken a significant step to prevent implementation of the Office of Management and Budget’s (OMB) proposed revisions to federal grant regulations. On 2 August, the Senate released the text of a Continuing Resolution to fund the federal government through mid-December. On the last page of the bill, Congress forbids the Administration from finalising or implementing OMB’s proposed revisions to grant regulations. The move follows sustained concern from research, higher education and scientific organisations about the potential impact on federal funding and research independence."

title: Change comes for science publishing paradigms | Science
content: How the Internet Disrupted Science tracks various changes in scientific publishing and the initiatives that have been undertaken to “disrupt” how science is published in scientific journals. Within science and technology fields, disruption is often framed as a positive change, one that shifts stale paradigms and allows new methods and theories to develop. In this book, authors Kent Anderson and Joy Moore present a much more negative view of disruption, arguing that the internet has set scientific publishing off track rather than enabling it to do more.
